article.title: Why More Features Can Make a Model Worse in Production
article.why: Practical analytical English for customer, experiment, and model decisions.

paragraphs.en:
Adding features often improves an offline model. More information can raise AUC or reduce loss, so teams are tempted to keep every variable that provides even a small gain. In production, however, each feature also creates operational cost and risk.

A feature may be predictive because it leaks information that does not exist at decision time. A status updated after a customer begins an application can predict completion very well, but it cannot support a campaign decision made before the application starts.

Availability is only one issue. Some features arrive late, fail intermittently, or require complicated joins across systems. A model with many upstream dependencies can break more often than a simpler model. Missingness can suddenly increase when one source changes.

Freshness matters too. A feature calculated monthly may be acceptable for a monthly campaign but unsuitable for a daily decision. Historical training data can contain perfectly reconstructed values while production scoring uses stale snapshots, creating a training-serving gap.

More features also increase governance burden. Teams must document definitions, owners, refresh schedules, privacy constraints, and transformation logic. When a source changes meaning, someone must detect the change and assess its effect.

Redundant variables can make explanations unstable. Correlated features may exchange importance across retraining runs even when predictions barely change. Extra complexity also makes debugging slower when scores suddenly move.

The right comparison is therefore not simply AUC with 50 features versus AUC with 200 features. Teams should compare end-to-end value: lift in the actionable population, decision-time availability, latency, pipeline reliability, monitoring burden, and maintenance cost.

Feature ablation is useful. Remove a group of variables and measure how much business-relevant performance changes. If a fragile source adds almost nothing to top-decile lift, removing it may improve the production system even if global AUC falls slightly.

Teams can classify features by operational criticality. Stable first-party transaction aggregates may be low risk, while externally sourced or complex cross-system variables may require stronger monitoring. This makes reliability an explicit design consideration rather than an afterthought.

Fallback behavior should also be designed. If a nonessential feature is temporarily unavailable, can the model score with a safe default, or must the entire pipeline stop? The answer affects service resilience and should be tested before deployment.

Production quality therefore includes reproducibility, timing, maintainability, and observability. A statistically stronger model that frequently misses the campaign deadline can create less business value than a slightly simpler model that scores every eligible customer reliably.

The best feature set is often the smallest set that preserves meaningful decision value while keeping operational risk under control. Offline metrics remain important, but they should be evaluated together with the engineering conditions required to deliver predictions consistently.
